title: Who's Up For A Circular Economy
summary: Josh and Chuck explain the circular economy, a model proposed largely through the Ellen MacArthur Foundation as an alternative to the linear take-make-waste economy. They cover design for longevity and repairability, planned obsolescence, recycling as a last resort, and examples including aluminum can recycling, Unilever refill programs, the Dutch companies Niaga (mattresses and carpets) and Bundles (appliance rental), food waste and the nutrient cycle, cascading food byproducts (Peel Pioneers), fast fashion's environmental impact, Patagonia and Infinna textile recycling, returns going to landfill, and right to repair. They end with a discussion of policy prospects in the US, the EU, and China, followed by listener mail correcting the Alexander Graham Bell birthplace and a shout-out to a listener.

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck joke about Jerry's lateness and about Stuff You Should Know not being on a Time magazine podcast list.

segments.title: Origins of the circular economy
segments.summary: Chuck explains the circular economy as a fairly new idea promoted by the Ellen MacArthur Foundation, with Ellen MacArthur's record solo sail around the world used as an aside. Outputs are meant to be reused as inputs, and recycling is considered among the least desirable options. A Deep Water documentary about Donald Crowhurst comes up in passing.

segments.title: The linear economy and its challenges
segments.summary: Josh describes the linear take-make-waste economy. Chuck explains that the linear model is profitable and has funded science and raised living standards, which makes shifting away from it difficult.

segments.title: Worst sectors and construction waste
segments.summary: The hosts name food, electronics, consumer goods, and construction as the worst sectors. They discuss planned obsolescence in electronics and clothing, and Josh recounts salvaging building materials from a renovation dumpster.

segments.title: What a circular economy aims to fix
segments.summary: Chuck says the circular model is conceptual and not a complete solution. Josh describes planned permanence, repairability, sharing and renting instead of owning, and recycling components at end of life. Chuck notes that reducing consumption is not emphasized.

segments.title: Repairing hammers and reuse
segments.summary: Using a hammer as an example, Chuck explains that reuse is better than recycling. Josh describes repair videos showing broken wooden hammer handles being fixed. Chuck issues a playful challenge to mail him broken hammers.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break.

segments.title: Aluminum cans and consumer behavior
segments.summary: Josh notes aluminum is highly recyclable, with about 71 percent recycled content in US cans. Chuck says about 35 percent of cans are still thrown away, so consumer behavior must change. They discuss corporate partnerships such as Unilever refill programs and small companies featured on Shark Tank with similar ideas.

segments.title: Niaga and medium-life bulky products
segments.summary: Chuck describes Dutch company Niaga, which targets carpets and mattresses as hard-to-recycle medium-life bulky products. Stats cited include about 20 million mattresses discarded in the US, 2 billion pounds of carpet landfilled, and only 5 percent of carpet recycled. Niaga makes mattresses from recyclable materials with replaceable parts.

segments.title: Design as the key to circularity
segments.summary: Josh argues that design is central, since linear products are purposefully made obsolete. Chuck adds that recycling infrastructure must be designed for products and that waste is a design choice, using packaging of potato chips as an example. Companies focused on the end user versus the broader environment are discussed.

segments.title: Milk-style delivery and energy inputs
segments.summary: Josh recalls Charles Chips reusable tin delivery service. Chuck notes that renewable energy alone cannot cover all needs, so industrial smoke stacks and power plants need to capture and reuse emissions.

segments.title: Product-as-a-service and Bundles appliance rental
segments.summary: Chuck describes Dutch company Bundles, which rents high-end appliances, installs and maintains them, and takes them back to refurbish. Customers pay per wash, tracked via Wi-Fi. Josh and Chuck discuss the American stigma of renting appliances and the cultural value of owning them.

segments.title: Laundry stain removers and tangent
segments.summary: The hosts joke about washing clothes and stain removers, including Shout and Zout. This section is mostly banter about laundry.

segments.title: Food waste and the nutrient cycle
segments.summary: Chuck says about a third of world food is wasted each year, worth about a trillion dollars. Josh explains that wasting food disrupts the natural nutrient cycle. Chuck notes that landfilling food removes nutrients from the cycle, and that composting is better.

segments.title: Biosolids and Milorganite
segments.summary: Chuck describes Milorganite, a fertilizer made from treated sewage biosolids from Milwaukee's municipal sewerage system, as a nitrogen-rich lawn fertilizer. Josh and Chuck joke about it and mention the Emily Sheep connection.

segments.title: Cascading food waste and anaerobic digesters
segments.summary: Josh describes cascading, reusing food byproducts, with Peel Pioneers in the Netherlands extracting essential oils from citrus peels. Converting waste to biofuel and anaerobic digesters with microbes that break down waste are also discussed.

segments.title: Fast fashion and textile recycling
segments.summary: The hosts describe fast fashion's labor, material, water, and emissions problems. Fashion is said to produce ten percent of global CO2 emissions, with 85 percent of clothing ending in landfills. Microplastics from washing are discussed. Patagonia's repair and resale programs and its partnership with Infinna, which recycles textile waste into a new fiber, are described. Clothing returns sent to landfill are also discussed.

segments.title: Right to repair and policy outlook
segments.summary: Josh explains the right to repair movement, including manufacturers' claims that repair manuals create hacking risks. Chuck describes his laptop battery that cannot be replaced. They doubt US implementation soon, note the EU's progress, and say global recycling is declining.

segments.title: Consumption growth and China's circular economy
segments.summary: Chuck cites data showing 500 gigatons of material consumed from 2018 to 2024 and that consumption keeps rising. He says China committed to a circular economy in the 2000s and currently focuses on automotive remanufacturing.

segments.title: Listener mail
segments.summary: Listener Joel corrects an earlier claim that Alexander Graham Bell was born in Branford, noting he was born in Scotland and only lived in Branford. The hosts also shout out listener Nick from Which Bolt.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Chuck gives the email address for contacting the show, and Josh closes with the iHeartRadio credit.
